[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Feature Scaling, Transformation, and Encoding in Data Science"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Data preprocessing is a critical step in building robust machine learning models. Raw data is often messy, unscaled, and contains categorical variables that algorithms cannot process natively. This tutorial covers the essential techniques of feature scaling, transformation, and encoding using Python and Scikit-Learn."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Feature Scaling"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Machine learning algorithms like gradient descent, support vector machines, and k-nearest neighbors are sensitive to the magnitude of features. If one feature has a range of 0 to 1,000,000 and another has a range of 0 to 1, the former will dominate the objective function. Feature scaling brings all numerical features onto a comparable scale."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Normalization (Min-Max Scaling): Rescales features to a fixed range, usually 0 to 1."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Standardization (Z-score Scaling): Centers the feature by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler
import numpy as np

data = np.array([[10, 2], [20, 4], [30, 6], [40, 8]])

# Min-Max Scaling
min_max_scaler = MinMaxScaler()
scaled_minmax = min_max_scaler.fit_transform(data)

# Standardization
standard_scaler = StandardScaler()
scaled_standard = standard_scaler.fit_transform(data)"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Feature Transformation"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Many machine learning models assume that numerical features are normally distributed. When data is heavily skewed, transformations such as the Log transformation or the Power Transformer (Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson) can stabilize variance and make the distribution more Gaussian."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

skewed_data = np.array([[1], [2], [10], [50], [200]])
pt = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson')
transformed_data = pt.fit_transform(skewed_data)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Categorical Encoding"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Algorithms require numerical inputs. Categorical variables (such as 'Red', 'Blue', 'Green' or 'Low', 'Medium', 'High') must be converted into numerical formats using encoding techniques."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Label Encoding: Converts categorical values into integer values (0, 1, 2). Best for ordinal data."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"One-Hot Encoding: Creates binary columns for each category. Best for nominal data to prevent the model from assuming an artificial ordering."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, LabelEncoder

# Label Encoding
le = LabelEncoder()
ordinal_data = ['Low', 'Medium', 'High', 'Low']
encoded_labels = le.fit_transform(ordinal_data)

# One-Hot Encoding
ohe = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False)
nominal_data = [['Red'], ['Blue'], ['Green'], ['Red']]
encoded_onehot = ohe.fit_transform(nominal_data)"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Properly scaling, transforming, and encoding your data ensures faster convergence in optimization algorithms and prevents biased model performance. Always fit your transformers on the training dataset and apply them to the validation and test sets to prevent data leakage."}]
